transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes (recording stopped at 15:52)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Tom Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Sable Head of Platform), Jared Miles (SRE), Lena Ortiz (Security), Ben Hsu (Engineer)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Demo focused on routing: org vs project keys, fairband/burst lanes, sticky routing, and quota carve-outs.
- Customer constraints: multi-tenant marketplace with bursty traffic, strict audit logs, and residency controls.
- Action: pilot to validate latency and cost tradeoffs using two project keys and Dedicated burst lanes; share pricing and compliance docs.

Topics: routing policies, org/project keys, quotas, Dedicated vs Hosted, Optimize suggestions, security & compliance

[00:00] Maya: yeah good afternoon everyone thanks for joining, um I'm Maya with Redwood, I'll kick things off and Tom who's here is our SE so we'll do a quick walkthrough of how we recommend mapping org and project keys for multi-tenant workloads.
[00:12] Priya: hey Maya, thanks. We have about 45 minutes for the demo and then 10 for logistics? That's the plan.
[00:17] Maya: yep perfect. Quick intro round? Tom, you want to go?
[00:20] Tom: yeah hey folks Tom Alvarez, I'm the solutions engineer working on routing and performance at Redwood. I'll jump into the console demo and then run through a sample live config.
[00:29] Jared: Jared here, SRE, mostly concerned about tail-latency and how we handle spikes from our marketplace sellers.
[00:34] Lena: Lena from security team, quick flag we need SOC2 evidence, KMS integration details, and SSO/SAML flow.
[00:40] Ben: Ben, eng - focus is cost and how to shape traffic into predictable lanes.

[02:05] Tom: okay quick context: Sable is a multi-tenant marketplace, right? You said heavy bursts when product launches, and some tenants are very latency-sensitive.
[02:14] Priya: exactly. Some enterprise sellers have SLA requirements, others are fine with slightly higher cost to reduce latency. We want to avoid noisy neighbors blowing our monthly spend.
[02:26] Tom: perfect. So our pattern today is org-level key + per-project keys. We typically advise keeping an org-level master key for admin automations and then per-tenant or per-product project keys for traffic shaping. That lets you apply quotas and routing at different levels.
[02:45] Maya: I'll show a high-level diagram first - sorry screen share - pulling up the Console.

[03:05] [Tom screen share begins - Console visible]
[03:12] Tom: top left is the org overview. You can see active projects, aggregated token usage, and latency percentiles. On the right we have routing policies - these are where fairband and burst lanes live.
[03:25] Ben: is fairband like a token bucket?
[03:28] Tom: it's similar conceptually - we call it fairband because it slices capacity across tenants and then we allow controlled bursts using dedicated lanes. The implementation is leaky-bucket-ish with priority lanes for high SLA keys.
[03:40] Priya: how do we do sticky routing? We need the same tenant to always hit their pinned model variant during a rollout.
[03:47] Tom: good Q - we have sticky routing rules tied to project keys. You can pin model variants at project-key level and add sticky TTLs. So if you pin a canary for tenant A, all requests with that project key will hit the canary until TTL expires or you toggle.
[04:03] Maya: also worth calling out fallback policies - if a dedicated lane is saturated we can route down to a hosted compatible model or lower-cost quantized variant automatically.

[04:15] Jared: what's the observable impact? Will our p95 jump when fallback happens?
[04:20] Tom: depends on model variant and sequence length. We show per-route latencies in the Console, and our traces tag whether request used fallback. In practice we see small variance but one thing Optimize provides is recommendations - if a fallback is causing regressions, we suggest changing batch/quant profiles.

[05:05] [05:05 - 07:20 rapid config demo, timestamps every ~30s]
[05:05] Tom: creating a new routing policy: call it "marketplace-priority". Source is project key X, priority = 80, fairband slice = 15% of org baseline, burst lane = enabled with 500 TPS burst cap.
[05:25] Ben: wait 500 TPS per tenant? That's per project key right?
[05:30] Tom: correct, it's per project key. You can also set org-wide caps that gate total org usage.
[05:36] Priya: can we set different affordability tiers - like low-cost for analytics, high-priority for shopper-facing?
[05:43] Tom: yes, create multiple project keys and reuse a routing policy tag. Analytics keys can be mapped to a "bulk" routing lane with more aggressive batching and a quantized model.

[07:50] Maya: quick aside on billing: tokens are billed by model variant and token direction. In the Console you can view token breakdowns per project key to attribute cost. That helps avoid noisy neighbors.

[08:30] Lena: about audit logs - we need immutable logs that show key usage and routing decisions. Is that out-of-the-box?
[08:38] Tom: yes we emit per-request audit logs with routing metadata, model variant used, latency, and tenant key. Logs can be archived to customer S3/Vault or integrated with your SIEM. Note: retention is configurable.
[08:52] Lena: KMS? Our policy says keys must be in our HSM.
[08:56] Maya: we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for data at rest and can integrate with your provider for encryption of stored artifacts. For in-flight encryption we use TLS - standard.

[09:30] [09:30 - 16:10 - deeper routing examples & mis-transcriptions]
[09:30] Tom: demo: I'll attach a second project key for a large seller, call it "enterprise-ACME" - this key will have a pinned model variant (redwood-2b-quant) and a higher priority lane.
[09:44] Ben: typo - ACME is used as a placeholder but we can swap with "Northridge" later.
[09:48] Tom: sure. Then I'll configure a carve-out quota: monthly cap 50M tokens but with a soft reserve guaranteeing 10% of org capacity. That means even during a heavy month they keep a minimum share.
[10:05] Priya: what's the enforcement? soft reserve vs hard cap?
[10:09] Tom: soft reserve uses prioritization to favor that key during contention; hard cap rejects requests with 429. You can also set adaptive backoff to return a hint so clients can retry later.
[10:21] Jared: do you support multi-region routing? We have EU-only data residency for some tenants.
[10:26] Tom: yes, routing policies can be scoped by region. You can pin a project key to EU nodes only; we honor data residency and will avoid routing cross-region.
[10:34] Maya: note: Private deployments give you VPC/on-prem control if needed for regulatory constraints.

[11:10] Priya: can we do rate-limits per user inside a project key? We have thousands of sellers under a single project key and want per-seller caps.
[11:18] Tom: you can issue sub-keys or use metadata-based sharding. We also have namespace-level enforcement - you can include seller-id in the header and configure per-namespace quotas. Caveat: if you want strict per-seller enforcement at scale, it's often easier to mint per-seller project keys automatically.

[12:05] [12:05 - 18:20 - Optimize suggestions and cost controls]
[12:05] Tom: switching to Optimize view - here we surface recommended quantization, batch sizes, and cache policies by workload. For example, for short prompt patterns we recommend prefix KV caching which reduced token spend 18% in a similar workload.
[12:25] Ben: prefix cache meaning cached KV cache?
[12:28] Tom: yes, prefix/KV caching - sometimes transcribed as KV cash in old notes - it keeps earlier activations to avoid recomputing. For many chat-like patterns it helps a lot.
[12:36] Priya: do we have automated suggestions for batch vs latency tradeoffs?
[12:40] Tom: Optimize provides a slider and simulated cost/latency curves. We can generate a few candidate configs and you can test them in the pilot.

[13:30] Maya: quick pause - any compliance blockers?
[13:33] Lena: SAMEL - SAML integration for our SSO is critical, plus review of pen-test reports.
[13:40] Maya: we'll include SAML docs and SOC2/ISO pack in the follow-up.

[14:05] [14:05 - 22:00 - Pilot topology discussion]
[14:05] Tom: recommended pilot: two project keys representing two tenant profiles: 1) "latency-sensitive" pinned to Dedicated lane with reserved capacity and burst enabled; 2) "bulk-analytics" mapped to hosted lane with quantized model and high batching. Run 48 hours of production-like traffic (we can replay traces) to collect p50/p95/p99 and token unit spend.
[14:30] Priya: what about our current infra - we use K8s + Envoy in front, can we integrate easily?
[14:36] Tom: yes standard sidecar or Envoy route header injection works. We have SDKs and examples. For high-throughput you can use Redwood's batching proxy but Envoy header is common.

[15:12] Jared: for the pilot what metrics do you need from us?
[15:15] Tom: traffic traces (headers), expected seq length distribution, SLOs per tenant, and a representative token mix. We'll instrument latency histograms and token cost.

[16:00] [16:00 - 30:10 - Q&A, objections, and tradeoffs]
[16:00] Ben: I'm worried about cost spikes if a tenant goes viral. Do we have hard budget guardrails per-account?
[16:08] Tom: yes - hard caps at project or org level will reject beyond threshold. Plus you can set budget notifications and auto-fallback to lower-cost models when approaching spend ceilings.
[16:25] Priya: and if we use Dedicated, can we still have org-wide fairband?
[16:30] Maya: Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools but routing still happens in the control plane. You can carve out dedicated capacity for a set of project keys and let others use shared hosted nodes.

[17:05] Lena: one more: auditability of routing decisions. We need per-request proof for auditors.
[17:12] Tom: we can export signed routing events with trace IDs and include them in audit bundles. We support long-term S3 retention and can provide indexing to help compliance teams search.

[18:00] [18:00 - 36:40 - live JSON config & small demo glitch]
[18:00] Tom: I'll paste an example policy JSON - bear with me. (Tom copies/pastes, small lag)
[18:05] Tom: "policy": {"match": {"project_key": "enterprise-ACME"}, "route": {"lane": "dedicated-priority", "reserve_pct": 10, "burst_cap": 500}}
[18:20] Ben: weird, the Console shows an extra zero on the burst cap in our view, maybe a typo?
[18:24] Tom: ah yes that was me entering 5000 accidentally, fixing to 500. Sorry about that.
[18:30] Maya: good catch. Live demos are humble.

[19:10] [19:10 - 26:00 - pilot logistics and data residency details]
[19:10] Priya: for EU-only tenants we will need to pin keys to eu-west nodes. Cost likely different?
[19:18] Tom: yes regional cost differs by region and model variant; Console shows region breakdowns. We'll include region pricing in the follow-up sheet.

[20:05] Jared: how do you reconcile client-side retries when a request is 429 vs fallback? We don't want clients hammering.
[20:12] Tom: we return standard rate-limit headers and an optional retry-after; we also provide adaptive backoff suggestions via the SDK so clients implement exponential jitter correctly.

[21:30] [26:00 - 34:00 - security deep-dive by Lena]
[26:00] Lena: can you run through the SSO flow quickly? We need to see SAML assertions and how RBAC maps to project keys.
[26:08] Tom: yes, in Console you map groups to project-key roles. SAML assertions are parsed and we map group attributes to RBAC. We also support SCIM provisioning to auto-provision users.
[26:34] Lena: about logs - are they tamper-evident?
[26:38] Tom: we provide signed audit logs and can enable an append-only storage backend; customers can ship logs to their own bucket for additional guarantees.

[28:15] Maya: sounds like we're aligned on the pilot. Quick recap of recommended pilot config: two project keys, Dedicated lane for latency-sensitive tenant with pinned model + reserve; Hosted lane for bulk analytics with quantized model + aggressive batching; 48 hour replay, metrics: p50/p95/p99, token cost, fallback rate.

[29:00] Priya: that works. Any blockers from you, Lena?
[29:05] Lena: no blockers; need compliance pack and proof of KMS integration.

[29:20] Maya: we'll attach docs in the follow-up and include a sample policy JSON, pricing sheet, and pilot runbook.

[30:00] [30:00 - 38:00 - closing discussion and scheduling]
[30:00] Tom: plan for next week: I'll share pilot config and we can schedule the infra pairing.
[30:10] Priya: we have a window starting Feb 1 to run the pilot - engineering availability then.
[30:18] Maya: great, I'll schedule a kickoff.

[31:05] Ben: small nit - what about eviction policy for caches under memory pressure?
[31:12] Tom: we expose cache eviction stats and implement LRU by default; Optimize suggests cache sizes based on your traffic.

[32:20] Jared: will you include runbook steps for fallback analysis? We want to run an incident like scenario to see behavior.
[32:26] Tom: yep - included in the pilot runbook.

[33:00] [33:00 - 40:50 - pricing & contract wrinkles]
[33:00] Maya: quick pricing note - Hosted billed per token; Dedicated includes reserved capacity fee plus usage. For billing we can set org-level billing alerts.
[33:18] Priya: for Dedicated do we commit monthly or yearly? And what about burst units?
[33:25] Maya: Dedicated is monthly or annual commit; burst is metered and billed separately but can be capped. We'll provide exact numbers in the spreadsheet.

[34:50] Lena: legal will want to see the SLA and data processing addendum.
[34:54] Maya: yes we'll share SLA + DPA.

[35:30] [40:50 - 51:30 - final recap and explicit next steps]
[40:50] Maya: final recap: Pilot config, pricing sheet, compliance pack. Tom will run the pilot config and share benchmark plan. Priya to confirm start date. Lena to collect compliance questions.
[41:05] Priya: all good, we'll aim to finalize ASAP.
[41:10] Maya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with notes and links.
[41:14] Jared: thanks.
[41:16] Ben: thank you.
[41:18] Lena: thanks.
